plan.title: AP Chemistry: Particles, Reactions & Equilibrium
plan.hook: Chemistry keeps coming back to counting: count protons and electrons to get charge, count moles against a balanced ratio to find what runs out, and compare two numbers — Q and K — to know which way a reaction will move.
objectives: Compute an ion's net charge from its proton and electron counts and state what fixes an element's identity
Use a balanced equation's mole ratios to identify the limiting reactant and any leftover excess
Explain how equal forward and reverse rates can hold unequal concentrations, and how comparing Q with K predicts the direction of net reaction
prerequisites: Basic ideas of atoms, elements, and chemical formulas

sections.heading: Charge counts particles, not atom size
points: Net charge is the difference between proton and electron counts
Proton count sets the element's identity
Electron count sets the charge — twelve protons and ten electrons give a net charge of +2

sections.heading: A balanced equation is a ratio
points: Coefficients in a balanced equation express mole ratios — 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O needs two H₂ per O₂
The limiting reactant runs out first relative to the balanced ratio and sets how many batches can run
Worked example: 8 H₂ with 3 O₂ makes 6 H₂O, leaves 2 H₂, and O₂ is limiting

sections.heading: Equal rates do not mean equal amounts
points: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal
Equal rates can maintain unequal, constant concentrations
Comparing Q with K at the same temperature predicts the direction of net reaction

sections.heading: Charge counts particles, not atom size
sections.body: Net charge follows the difference between proton and electron counts. Element identity depends on proton count.
sections.visual: Twelve positive proton charges and ten negative electron charges leave a net charge of +2.

questions.q: An ion has 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its net charge, and why?
questions.hint: Subtract the electron count from the proton count.
questions.answer: The net charge is +2, because net charge follows the difference between proton and electron counts: 12 − 10 = +2.

questions.q: Which count decides what element an atom is, and which decides its charge?
questions.hint: The diagram separates the two jobs: one count names the element, the other sets the charge.
questions.answer: Proton count sets the element's identity. Electrons set the charge, because charge comes from the imbalance between protons and electrons.

sections.heading: A balanced equation is a ratio
sections.body: In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, coefficients express mole ratios. The limiting reactant runs out first relative to the balanced ratio.
sections.visual: The balanced reaction needs two H₂ for each O₂. Eight H₂ and three O₂ allow three batches: six H₂O form and two H₂ remain.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="The limiting reactant sets the number of batches"><title>The limiting reactant sets the number of batches</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">The limiting reactant sets the number of batches</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="80" y="100" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="18">2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O</text><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="160" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="18">Start: 8 H₂ · 3 O₂</text></g><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="210" fill="#ffd479" font-size="18">Need 2 H₂ per O₂</text></g><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="260" fill="#b39dff" font-size="18">3 batches use 6 H₂ + 3 O₂</text></g><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="310" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="18">Make 6 H₂O · 2 H₂ left over</text></g><rect x="480" y="100" width="260" height="200" rx="12" fill="#172331" stroke="#344253"/><text x="500" y="140" fill="#ffd479" font-size="17">Limiting: O₂</text><text x="500" y="180" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Runs out first</text><text x="500" y="230" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="17">Excess: H₂</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Balanced equation is a ratio of batches</text></svg>

questions.q: In 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, what do the coefficients tell you?
questions.hint: They are not just bookkeeping — read them as a recipe ratio.
questions.answer: They express mole ratios: the reaction consumes two H₂ for every one O₂ and produces two H₂O. The balanced equation is a ratio of batches.

questions.q: Starting with 8 H₂ and 3 O₂, which reactant is limiting and what remains?
questions.hint: Count how many full batches each reactant can support at the 2:1 ratio.
questions.answer: O₂ is limiting: 3 O₂ support three batches, using 6 H₂ and all the O₂ to make 6 H₂O. Two H₂ are left over in excess.

sections.heading: Equal rates do not mean equal amounts
sections.body: Equal forward and reverse rates can maintain unequal, constant concentrations. Comparing Q with K predicts direction of net reaction.
sections.visual: At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates match even when amounts differ.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Equal rates, unequal amounts"><title>Equal rates, unequal amounts</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Equal rates, unequal amounts</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="200" y="180" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="28">X</text><text x="400" y="180" fill="#ffd479" font-size="22">⇌</text><text x="600" y="180" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="28">Y</text><path d="M250 200 L350 200" stroke="#7cc7ff" stroke-width="3" class="lw-flow"/><path d="M550 220 L450 220" stroke="#7ee2a8" stroke-width="3" class="lw-flow"/><text x="400" y="280" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle">Rates equal · amounts need not be</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Compare Q with K at the same temperature</text></svg>

questions.q: At equilibrium the amounts of X and Y are unequal, yet nothing seems to change. How?
questions.hint: Separate the sizes of the amounts from the speeds of the two reactions.
questions.answer: The forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations stay constant — but equal rates do not require equal amounts. The two concentrations can sit at different, steady values.

questions.q: What comparison tells you which way a reaction will move toward equilibrium?
questions.hint: The diagram names two quantities to compare at the same temperature.
questions.answer: Compare Q with K. Their relative sizes predict the direction of net reaction needed to reach equilibrium.

questions.q: A particle has 12 protons and 10 electrons. Its net charge and identity are determined as follows:
choices: Net charge +2; the 12 protons set the element
Net charge −2; the 10 electrons set the element
Net charge +2; the larger atom size sets the element
Net charge 0; protons and electrons cancel by count of atoms
questions.explain: Net charge follows the difference between proton and electron counts: 12 − 10 = +2. Element identity depends on proton count — electrons set the charge, not the element, and atom size plays no part.

questions.q: Two ions have the same number of protons but different numbers of electrons. What must be true?
choices: They are different elements with the same charge
They are the same element with different charges
They are the same element with the same charge
They cannot both exist as ions
questions.explain: Proton count sets the element, so equal protons means the same element. Different electron counts change the proton–electron difference, so the charges differ.

questions.q: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, you start with 8 H₂ and 3 O₂. How much H₂O forms and what is left over?
choices: 8 H₂O, nothing left over
6 H₂O, with 2 H₂ left over
4 H₂O, with 3 O₂ left over
6 H₂O, with 2 O₂ left over
questions.explain: The ratio needs 2 H₂ per O₂, so 3 O₂ run three batches: they use 6 H₂ and make 6 H₂O. O₂ runs out first — it is limiting — and 2 H₂ remain in excess.

choices: Has the smallest mass in the mixture
Runs out first relative to the balanced ratio
Appears last in the balanced equation
Has the smallest coefficient in the equation
questions.explain: The limiting reactant runs out first relative to the balanced ratio, and that caps how many batches can run. In the worked example O₂ is limiting even though the mixture holds more H₂ by count.

questions.q: At equilibrium, a mixture holds much more Y than X, and both amounts stay constant. This is possible because…
choices: The forward reaction has stopped
The reverse reaction has stopped
Forward and reverse rates are equal even though amounts are not
Both reactions continue but only in one direction at a time
questions.explain: Equal forward and reverse rates maintain the concentrations, and those rates can match while the amounts stay unequal. Neither reaction stops; they balance.

questions.q: To predict the direction of net reaction for a mixture, you compare…
choices: The amounts of products and reactants directly
Q with K at the same temperature
The forward rate with the starting concentration
The temperature with the equilibrium constant alone
questions.explain: The section and diagram both name the comparison: Q against K, at the same temperature, predicts the direction of net reaction.

sections.title: Protons name it, electrons charge it
bullets: Net charge = proton count − electron count.
12 protons and 10 electrons leave a net charge of +2.
Proton count sets the element; electrons set the charge.
sections.notes: Charge is a counting problem, not a size problem. Count positive protons, count negative electrons, and subtract. The proton count alone tells you which element you have; the imbalance tells you the charge.
sections.visual: Twelve positive proton charges and ten negative electron charges leave a net charge of +2.

sections.title: A balanced equation is a ratio
bullets: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O: two H₂ are needed for each O₂.
The limiting reactant runs out first relative to that ratio.
8 H₂ + 3 O₂ → three batches: 6 H₂O formed, 2 H₂ left over.
sections.notes: Read the coefficients as a recipe ratio. Three oxygens can only partner with six hydrogens at two-to-one, so oxygen caps the run at three batches — six waters — and the extra hydrogen simply stays behind.
sections.visual: The balanced reaction needs two H₂ for each O₂. Eight H₂ and three O₂ allow three batches: six H₂O form and two H₂ remain.

sections.title: Equal rates, unequal amounts
bullets: At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates match.
Concentrations stay constant without having to be equal.
Compare Q with K at the same temperature to predict the direction of net reaction.
sections.notes: Equilibrium is a balance of speeds, not of amounts. Both reactions keep running at the same rate, so the mixture holds steady — and the Q-versus-K comparison tells you which way it will drift to get there.
sections.visual: At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates match even when amounts differ.

enrichment.audioTitle: AP Chemistry: Particles, Reactions & Equilibrium — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: This course is three counting problems. First: an ion with 12 protons and 10 electrons. What is its net charge?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Twelve plus ten is twenty-two... no — charge is the difference, so +2?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Right — net charge follows the difference between proton and electron counts: 12 − 10 = +2. And what makes it the element it is — the protons or the electrons?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: A common mix-up. Element identity depends on proton count. Electrons set the charge precisely because they are the count that can differ.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: So same protons, different electrons: same element, different charge.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly. Second problem: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, starting with 8 H₂ and 3 O₂. How many batches can run?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Each batch needs two H₂ per O₂. Three O₂ need six H₂, so three batches — 6 H₂O, and 2 H₂ left over.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: O₂ — it runs out first relative to the ratio, even though there is more H₂ around.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Good. Third problem: at equilibrium the amounts of X and Y are unequal but constant. How can both be true?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: If the reactions stopped, amounts would freeze — but one side has more, so maybe only the bigger side stopped?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Neither side stops. The forward and reverse rates are equal, so the concentrations hold steady — equal rates do not mean equal amounts.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: And to know which way a mixture will move, compare Q with K at the same temperature.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That is the whole course in one line: count charges, count batches against the ratio, and compare Q with K.

nodes.label: AP Chemistry: Particles, Reactions & Equilibrium
nodes.note: Charge, reaction yield, and equilibrium direction all come from counting the right things.

nodes.label: Charge from counts
nodes.note: Net charge is the difference between proton and electron counts.

nodes.label: Protons set the element
nodes.note: Element identity depends on proton count; electrons set the charge.

nodes.label: Equations as ratios
nodes.note: Balanced coefficients express mole ratios between reactants and products.

nodes.label: Limiting reactant
nodes.note: The reactant that runs out first relative to the ratio caps the batches: 8 H₂ + 3 O₂ make 6 H₂O with 2 H₂ left.

nodes.label: Equal rates, unequal amounts
nodes.note: At equilibrium forward and reverse rates match while concentrations stay constant and possibly unequal.
